speechtext:

subsubtopic: TERMS OF AGREEMENT TO SELL URANIUM AND NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY TO JAPAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question arises from reports that an agreement between Canada and Japan is soon to be signed, within the next two weeks, regarding the sale of uranium and nuclear technology. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is quoted as saying that the embargo on sales of uranium to Japan may be raised as early as next week. Therefore it seems to me that it is important that the House be given some information regarding this agreement.
My question is, therefore, to the Secretary of State for External Affairs or to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, whichever is more familiar with the terms of the agreement. In view of the fact that there are two basic items in the report regarding the agreement, one to do with keeping the level enriched uranium to 20 per cent and the other to do with the right of Canada to veto any transfer of uranium or nuclear technology to a third country, both of which would require very strong monitoring to ensure that there is no violation, I want to ask either of the ministers-whether the proposed agreement will leave the monitoring entirely to the IAEA or whether Canada reserves the right to on-site inspection by Canadian officials? If so, does the government intend to exercise that right?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall do my best to satisfy you on the point. I realize that ministers do not have to answer questions in the House of Commons: they can answer questions facetiously, evade them, or avoid them. It is unfortunate that this is permitted under our rules. I rose primarily because that is what happened today. Ministers can, of course, do that if they wish. However, this issue is of such significance that that practice ought not to have happened.
It is important that parliament and the people of this country understand that in terms of the rules of this House and the way we operate, there is a way in which this matter can be brought before parliament. Quite frankly, that is the approach the government adopted when they wanted to proclaim the Official Languages Act. They found a way to do that. A resolution was brought forward asking for an expression of parliament's views on the matter. That was a very
Oral Questions
historic occasion. I was impressed with the imagination of the government at that time.
Another way to deal with the matter would be to table the reports and allow them to be presented to a committee of the House of Commons, either a special committee-a select committee or a joint committee. There is another method. They could bring in a bill, as they did with the James Bay agreement and a whole host of other matters, incorporating in the bill the draft agreement, which would allow the House to pass on the matter. Even though this may not deal with a specific provision of the Standing Orders, it deals with an important and fundamental aspect of the operation of the parliamentary system in Canada. It is such a fundamental operation that no government, however well-intentioned-and I do not suspect that of this government-ought to be allowed to rely on the excuse that parliament may not be sitting when a decision has to be made. Your Honour, as Speaker of this House of Commons, has the power at any time to summon parliament to deal with a particular matter.
In my experience here of almost five years parliament has been summoned back on matters of emergency on several occasions. We have taken the unfortunate step-it is unfortunate in terms of the process of collective bargaining-of biting the bullet as a parliament and legislating people back to work because there was an emergency. It was done after proper consultation between the then government House leader and the opposition House leader. On one occasion I was involved in those consultations.
This parliament is not bound by its recesses. It ought to be bound by its traditions. One tradition of this place ought to be upheld: objection should be taken on every occasion when there is a danger that it will not be upheld. Parliament ought to deal with matters openly, fairly and concisely, and the people ought to have the opportunity to enter into debate through this parliament and its processes, processes which are available to it and the government in this very fundamental decision.
I feel very strongly about this matter. I was concerned about it before the exchange between the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the government. I am much more concerned about what I see happening in the course of events that I see unfolding in view of the answers given by the government House leader. As government House leader, he has a particular responsibility above all other parliamentarians-except Your Honour-to ensure that this House of Commons operates in such a way that matters of this nature are brought to the attention of the House.
I want to say something else, through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I hope the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, as he looks upon this parliament, looks upon it not merely as a place where the adversary interest is highest but as one in which the government, in the course of makings decisions, can call upon the help of members of parliament who represent large areas of the country. I am glad to see he agrees. The decisions eventually reached might be better for the government and, more

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a fundamental difference between what the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton has been talking about and what the President of the Privy Council has been talking about. The President of the Privy Council has, intentionally or not, sidestepped the whole issue. He says, first of all, that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has referred the matter of an energy strategy for Canada to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. This
Committee, I would point out, covers the whole field of oil, gas, uranium, nuclear reactors and hydro power.
I would point out that so far we have received no report from the National Energy Board. The minister keeps saying we are jumping the gun when we talk about the Mackenzie Valley pipeline because we have not yet received the report of the National Energy Board. Therefore, the fact that energy policy is being discussed by a committee does not mean that parliament is involved with reference to a final decision on the pipeline.
The minister says, too, that the report of Mr. Justice Berger could be referred to a committee of the House. I think it should be. But I would point out that this report does not constitute a recommendation either to build a pipeline or not to build it. The commission was set up for the purpose of informing the government with regard to the environmental aspects, the dislocating effects on the native people, and so on. Its findings should, of course, be taken into consideration when making a final decision, but the final decision will arise out of the report of the National Energy Board. If it is a favourable report, the cabinet will decide whether or not to accept a recommendation to grant a permit to build a pipeline.
The minister is simply beclouding the issue when he talks about legislation. He knows perfectly well that legislation might very well be brought down after the permit is given. It could be a conditional permit. Later, legislation could be brought in-for example, if there were a question of financial guarantees-but there need be no legislation prior to the decision to grant a permit to build a pipeline, if that is the recommendation of the board.
When the report of the National Energy Board is received, a committee of the House ought to have an opportunity to examine it. That, to my mind, is clear. The government ought to have an opportunity to make its decision. The matter should then be placed before parliament. After all, this is a question affecting the lives of the native people and the environment of the Arctic, as well as having large economic implications- perhaps $10 billion or $12 billion. If the companies concerned ask for financial guarantees, it could be many billions of dollars more. This will have tremendous repercussions for Canada, and the possibility of such a decision being made simply in the executive council seems to me to be a negation of everything we have ever held to be democratic and parliamentary.
I recognize the limitations upon the President of the Privy Council. He must, of course, consult the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the cabinet generally. I think he and his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, agree in their hearts that this matter should come before parliament. I hope this opinion will be shared by the rest of the ministers in the cabinet.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF WET SNOW ON RADAR
speechtext: Does wet snow affect radar and, if so (a) in what manner (b) how is this undesirable effect reduced or eliminated by DOT or DND radar installations?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF WET SNOW ON RADAR
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of National Defence is concerned: Yes. (a) Effects of wet snow on radar include: The possibility of damage to the antenna system unless covered by radomes; Attenuation of the radar energy to and from the target; Clutter returns (backscatter). However, snow only has an effect which at most is comparable to, and normally less significant than, rain, (b) Using lower frequencies to ensure that path attenuation has no significant effect on target detection. To reduce the level of backscatter received one or more of the following techniques are used: pulse coding, pulse compression or shorter pulse operation; smaller beam width, more directional antennae or multiple beam antennae. To reduce or eliminate backscatter returns after reception, the following signal processing schemes are used: Circuitry which prevents saturation by high level clutter returns; Circuitry which removes the mean value of the background clutter; and moving target indication techniques which eliminate stationary or slow moving clutter. In addition to the above, all DND surveillance radars have Identification Friend or Foe/Secondary Surveillance Radar (IFF/SSR) facilities which complement primary radar returns and IFF/SSR is virtually unaffected by weather clutter.
In so far as Transport Canada is concerned: (a) Wet, falling snow can impair the performance of Radar. Wet snowflakes reflect transmitted radar energy back to the receiver as radar
April 22, 1977

echoes. If the snowfall rate is intense, the reflected energy from each snowflake combine and appear as one large echo on a radar display. Therefore, an echo from an aircraf flying in this snowfall would be completely obscured, (b) DOT Aircraft-Surveillance Radars overcome this undesirable effect by: (1) Using low radar frequencies (L-band) which penetrate wet snow more readily than higher frequencies. (2) Transmitting and receiving radar energy using circular polarization which suppresses echoes from wet snow, but not aircraft. (3) Using moving target indicator (MTI) circuitry which cancels stationary or low velocity echoes and not the high velocity aircraft echoes. In all except the most severe snowfall conditions, these techniques eliminate the undesirable effect of wet snow. It should be noted that the reflectivity of wet snow increases with an increase in frequency of the energy radiated from a radar. This phenomenon is taken advantage of in weather radars maintained by DOT for Environment Canada, Atmospheric Environment Services. Weather radars operate at approximately three times the frequency of aircraft-surveillance radars and thus readily detect the presence of a weather system that contains wet snow.

Scientific Activities of Government

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURES RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, December 13, 1976, consideration of the motion of Mr. Faulkner (for the Prime Minister) that Bill C-26, respecting the organization of certain scientific activities of the government of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURES RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I last had the opportunity to speak on Bill C-26 1 was pointing out to the House that Canada faces a very serious trade imbalance with respect to the manufacture and export of relatively high technology products. In fact, we quoted figures which had already been put before the House showing that that imbalance was approximately $8.2 billion. I suggest that one of the reasons we are living with imbalances of that magnitude is that this government has been out of touch with reality so far as the importance of research and development is concerned, especially in industrial terms, throughout the world.
I think it is most regrettable that a review of the figures supplied, not by this government but by the government of the United States, reveals how poorly Canada fares in relation to research and development budgets compared to other countries of the world. The last time I spoke I referred to the international economic report of the President which was transmitted to the Congress of the United States in March, 1976. This kind of information is not available in Canada, for some reason. On page 119 of that American report it is stated, for example, that research and development expenditures, as a percentage of the gross national product in 1963 and 1973, the two years that were compared, amounted to .3 per cent of the gross national product in Canada, whereas in the United States, for the same period, the total funding of research and development in industry amounted to 1 per cent. In other words, the Americans spent more than three times as much on research and development than we did in the two years to which I have referred.
As for funding by government, the same lack of attention was shown in Canada in the two years to which I have referred. Funding on research and development, as a percentage of the gross national product, in Canada was between one-third to one-half of the comparable level in the United States. Other countries also show how deficient we have been in this respect. For example, in 1973, compared to our .3 per cent of the gross national product being funded by industry for research and development, France spent twice as much. West Germany spent 1.4 per cent of its gross national product, as did Japan, compared to our .3 per cent. In the same year, 1973, the United Kingdom spent .8 per cent. In short, every

country listed in the report which was submitted to the United States Congress was well ahead of Canada in terms of expenditure on research and development, both on the part of government and on the part of industry.
That is why we on this side of the House are saying that it is time the government was alerted and got in touch with reality. What is the point of the Minister of Finance decrying in his budget speech the fact that we have an end product trade deficit at the present time of over $10 billion? What is the point of emphasizing that and, so far as research and development are concerned, allowing the deficiency to which I have referred to continue?
Mr. Speaker, this deficiency can be corrected very quickly. Surely the government realizes this. The fact is that one of our problems in this country is that we have a disproportionate amount of our industry controlled by those who are resident in foreign countries. That is known. The fact that it is known does not mean that the government cannot take action to ensure that we get our pro rata share of research and development which is being conducted by the multinational corporations concerned. If the American parent, the United Kingdom parent or the West German parent of a Canadian company intends to spend $1 million on research and development, surely we should, through moral suasion, if not by other means, make sure that that multinational corporation gives a percentage of the research and development activity to the subsidiary that is carrying on business in Canada.
I would like to hear representatives of the government comment on that matter. To what extent have they tried to use moral suasion to ensure that we get a better slice of the research and development activity that is taking place in multinational corporations which have subsidiaries in this country? I was shocked to hear that the then minister of state for science and technology said, when this point was raised, that somehow Canadians were well off. He said we got the advantage of the research and development that was being carried out by multinational corporations. We got the spillover, in effect. How ridiculous!
The minister was indicating that Canada should be second-class and should only receive the used material after the original research and development had been obviously exploited by the country which originally carried it out at the parent company level. That is not good enough. If we wish to enhance our position in the world as far as the manufacture of our high-technology goods is concerned, we must ensure that there is in this country a pro rata share of the research and development which is being carried on, in order to allow us to catch up with the rest of the world and not fall farther behind.
When the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) spoke on this bill initially, as I recall it he said that the chief thrust of the legislation was to deal with federal support of research in the nation's universities. We have no particular quarrel with that. He went on to say that he promised to have more to say at another time about support of
April 22, 1977

industrial research and research in the government's own laboratories.
The transfer of research and technology to the manufacturing sector remains one of the nation's most pressing problems. The hard figures show that our industries are not as competitive in world markets as they should be. I have referred to the figures we have received from the Americans. I also point out that it has been noted that in France, West Germany, Japan, The Netherlands, and Sweden the average is that about 25 persons per 10,000 are engaged in industrial research and development. In Canada the figure is only eight persons per 10,000. In short, only about a third of our working force is engaged in some type of research and development in industry.
The Science Council of Canada, in report No. 24 of December, 1975, when discussing the critical shortage of industrial research in Canada said at page 8:
New technology is one of the essential components of industrial innovation, and it has been long recognized that there is a need for much more innovation in Canadian industry. The issue has now become an extremely urgent one. Manufacturing industry in Canada is disturbingly weak and dominated by foreign firms. When so many other nations with resource-based economies are putting such new emphasis on strengthening their own manufacturing sectors, we cannot afford to be left behind. The time to act decisively is now, before our unfavourable technological situation deteriorates any further.
The report, after criticizing the government's lack of interest in transferring technology to the manufacturing sector, says the chief aims of government research in this country have been directed to the primary industries-agriculture, fishing, forestry. At page 10 the report strongly urges the government to "stimulate innovation in secondary manufacturing industry". Rather than heed this advice from the Science Council of Canada back in 1975-there were even earlier warnings of declining industrial innovation in 1968-the government chose to bring before us the bill we are now debating, which accomplishes little more than a bureaucratic reshuffling of administrators. I am referring to report No. 2 entitled "Toward a National Science Policy". An additional layer of advisers is not what this country needs to compete more effectively in a market which demands ever-increasing technological sophistication.
Nowhere in the vague generalities of the minister's opening comments on this bill is there any indication of the government's understanding of the seriousness of the situation to which I have referred. In fact, the only concrete action to be taken by Bill C-26 is that it will increase the number of councils from four to six, with four of these to be directly engaged in granting schemes. In the segregation of the granting functions by scientific fields and the proliferation of administrative staff necessary to implement this bill, the goal of cycling more money into research, principally industrial research, becomes even further removed.
My colleague, the hon. member for Athabsca (Mr. Yew-chuk) has pointed to the model of an integrated granting agency such as the United States national science foundation as offering the advantage of utilizing common management and financial services with substantial savings in administrative costs. Under Bill C-26 we are redistributing our already
Scientific Activities of Government meagre allotment of funds for research among a great number of administrative bodies, with even less eventually to be used in research.
The government's total budget for all scientific research in Canada amounts to only $160 million. This represents only about 40 per cent of the level of the scientific funding of other western nations.

It makes better sense to spend more money finding cures for those diseases, as opposed to simply trying to come up with schemes to look after people when they have contracted the disease.
The main thrust of what I am saying is one of the most imperative problems facing this nation; that is, our trade imbalance. Economically, this country is not prospering. We have had a trade deficit in the last few years which in the aggregate is greater than the trade deficit of the United Kingdom, the United States, West Germany, Japan, France and Italy together. Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate briefly in the debate on second reading of this bill. I am pleased to see that the minister is in the chamber, accompanied by the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine), who before he entered parliament was well known for his scientific activity and his great interest in scientific matters. I see the minister has the hon. member seated next to him, possibly to obtain advice and counsel on this legislation.
One of the reasons I enter this debate is that I want to deal with the facet of the bill which concerns new social sciences and humanities research. Before the bill goes to committee- which for some reason, I understand, is the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates-I want to raise some matters so that in committee we may be able to obtain answers and perhaps undertakings which would sit well with people interested in this aspect of the bill, particularly with the academic community.
The government is correct in saying, as it did in the background information fact sheet, that during the last few years a number of studies have been made of the manner in which research moneys are to be distributed in the area of social sciences and the humanities. Various bodies, learned societies and research councils have recommended a split in the existing Canada Council. This split would have the effect of leaving the arts division of the Canada Council as the only part of a restructured council, and taking away from it and setting up as a separate research body the humanities and social sciences division of the existing council.
A number of reports have been prepared and studies have been made, including the Timlin report, by Mabel Timlin of Saskatchewan whose memory is so revered there; the Macdonald report; the OECD report; the Lamontagne report, by Senator Lamontagne who was a keen advocate of this legislation; the Humanities Research Council of Canada report; and the Social Sciences Research Council of Canada report. The last two bodies are not granting agencies but are federations of many learned societies. They tend to promote professional interests and to support academic publications, but as I understand it they do not overlap the research activities of the Canada Council.
There are, of course, those who have not been entirely enthusiastic about this legislation. The minister will be aware of the statement of Gertrude Laing and editorials by people who might have a particular interest in the Canada Council. I will allow the minister to make his reply in his own thorough manner, Mr. Speaker. What is not clear, given the desire for the split on the part of so many bodies and societies, is the implication for research in the humanities and social sciences under a new granting agency with a different set of relationships to the government. I think this, with great respect, is what concerns a fairly substantial number of people within the academic community.
I should also like to hear from the minister at the committee stage what the reorganization cost will be. This is important at a time when we as parliamentarians, regardless of party, are concerned with restraint in government spending and the cost of government. I think it also concerns a substantial number of people within the academic community, and the minister should address himself to it. I have heard estimates of from $750,000 to $1 million.
I should also like the minister to elaborate on the basis of the split and the way in which it has been done. I raise this matter in the context of splitting the arts from the other pursuits of the new council. I do not know if it is unfair to artists to say they are generally, or even notoriously, naive in political and governmental affairs. The artistic temperament is sometimes said not to include business ability or to be able to articulate support for their own enterprises or to deal with the labyrinth of government bureaucracy in order to acquire funds for worth while projects. Be that as it may there is concern that the arts may lose more from this split than the social sciences and the humanities, because they will be on their own when it comes to obtaining funds.
The model for the proposed sciences and humanities research council is the Medical Research Council, a body which was hived off from the National Research Council a few years ago. According to reports which I have, the Medical Research Council was tailor-made for its first president. I question the wisdom of adopting a model from one area of scientific inquiry as an appropriate model for another. This should be self-evident to anyone who thinks seriously about the nature of scientific research in both the humanities and the social sciences.
These are points I want to raise at committee. I raise them for the minister now so that he will be prepared to answer them and to see if provision can be made for amendment to the bill. Let me give a small example. Under section 6(1) and (2) and section 8, the bill on organization, the president is to be a full-time paid person of the commission. He is to be appointed for a five-year term. Yet no provision is made for a full-time vice-president who would taker over in the event the president

April 22, 1977

is incapacitated. There might be some merit in making this additional appointment to ensure the continuity of activities within the council.
The structure and constitution of the council are of far greater import. Because of the nature of the subject matter, social scientists and humanists often pursue research matters that are controversial and, indeed, politically embarrassing on occasion, or politically dangerous. Their search for truth and their pursuit of verifiable facts, in my submission, makes independence from government control essential. The present Canada Council, I suggest, is structured in such a way. But if under the new legislation the council, appointed by the government for three-year terms, is made up of specialists and professionals in the social sciences and humanities, no buffer would exist, as at present with the academic advisory panel, between the academics and what is sometimes termed the cruel outside world.
The current council has a mixed lay and specialist membership. It is not really made up of practitioners of the trade, that is to say, academics; rather, it has a nice balance of business, professional, artistic and academic people. If the new council were to be made up of academics alone, then we would certainly be seen, whenever anything controversial came up, to be protecting their vested interests. I think the matter is still important enough to raise, that is to say, the need to have an advisory body below the council, free of government, not appointed by the government but, rather, by the council on recommendations of universities, learned societies, and so on, and able to exercise independent judgment on academic matters.
I think the most important matter has to do with the possibility of the government referring matters to the new council. There has been some reaction to this question by the minister, but the reference of matters by the government to the new council for research is most important. Under the present system it is my understanding that such could not be the case. Under the proposed legislation, section 16(1), the new body will be made "an agent of Her Majesty". I would like to obtain from the minister a clarification, not only on the record, but an assurance that he will look at the drafting of the legislation to make certain that the term "an agent of Her Majesty" will not be misunderstood. This may be a totally innocuous phrase and may simply be dismissed as a legal nicety to ensure our transfer to a new category B, similarily to a department, subject to the Civil Service Act, the Financial Administration Act, and so on. It may, however, have deeper meaning in that the government could refer matters to the new council for research.
I think, also, that along these lines we should look specifically at the wording of section 5(l)(b) which relates to the minister "referring". The minister himself, in the course of a news release around the early part of December-December 2, I believe-said he would request funds for council programs relating to regional balance, national problem areas and inter-
Scientific Activities of Government disciplinary research. This could well constitute interference in the affairs of the new body, for it must be independent to support the sort of research it feels-through its own elaborate evaluation system, I grant you-warrants support on the basis of this evaluation process, rather than whatever the government of the day decides is appropriate research to be carried out by the council.
The new council may well support studies relating to regional balance, etc., but I repeat that this would only come after it had received applications and assessed them through the normal evaluation routes. The government has 29 or 30 departments to study regional balance, so why should it have to turn the new agency into yet another? Even if the minister says he is not going to do so, the potential is there, given the suggested relationship between the government and the council in the bill.
On the matter of evaluation procedures, the Canada Council now has elaborate and well developed procedures. They have much to be proud of in those procedures and, I suggest, they are the envy of granting agencies in other countries. But they are necessarily different from those used by the Medical Research Council and, indeed, the National Research Council, at least in some respects. Does the government intend, not so much through the legislation as through the powers available to it under the Financial Administration Act and through the Treasury Board, to force upon the new council different ways of assessing research applications? I would very much appreciate the minister, in the course of his deliberations in committee, telling us the policy of the government in this connection.

I think it is important and of interest to put on the record some of the suggestions made by that panel with respect to any restructuring of the Canada Council as contemplated by this legislation. These recommendations were made after the intention of the government was announced in the Speech from the Throne starting the session of 1974 and, as we all know, it has

Scientific Activities of Government taken since then for this bill to come to this point. However, it has been the intention of the government for some time to restructure the activities of the Canada Council. The position of the advisory academic panel is stated in the following recommendation:
The present programs and methods of operation of the Humanities and Social Sciences Division of the Canada Council have evolved out of the needs of the disciplines it serves. Research in these disciplines varies greatly in subject matter, methods and organizational needs. It is sometimes controversial and is often of immediate significance for questions of public policy. For the benefit of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), pro tem who is now in the chamber-my geographical but not political friend, I should add-I am pointing out some of the observations of the advisory academic panel which underline, 1 think, the point I was making earlier. The advisory academic panel went on to make certain specific recommendations which I would like to bring to the attention of the House. One of the recommendations was as follows:
That the new council be empowered to act as a board of public trustees, and to this end should include laymen as well as scholars. It will be necessary for the new council to exercise policy judgments and a degree of external control which a body composed only of professionals could not visibly exercise.
It seems to me that a mix of professionals and laymen is a very worthwhile objective which we would all support so there could not be the suggestion that a group, panel or body comprising exclusively professionals or academics in a particular area would be involved in self-service but, rather, that the general point of view was being expressed in an independent way. The recommendations went on to point out the following:
That the present system of evaluation of research projects through the use of external assessors be retained.
Prior to one o'clock I mentioned the desirability of having this kind of structure below the council which would be available to recommend policy as far as the council was concerned. I want to conclude my remarks by referring to a point of view expressed in an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of December 20, 1976, because I think it underlines some of the objections and points of view which have been taken by a fairly substantial number of people across Canada. I commend this editorial to the minister for the purpose of discussion in committee. The editorial was written by John W. Grace, who has had a long association with the Canada Council and, therefore, has knowledge of the past workings of that body. It is important, therefore, for the committee to consider these opinions when discussing the structure of the proposed council. The editorial reads in part:
[Mr. Hnatyshyn.)
The Canada Council has two integral functions from its creation about 20 years ago. The more visible function has been the funding of the arts in Canada ... the less publicly recognized council activity has been the support for university research in the humanities and the social sciences;...
Bill C-26-
That is the bill we are now discussing-
-would hive off the second function and make that the responsibility of a new council to be called the social science and humanities research council. The present Medical Research Council would inherit NRC's historic responsibility for support for the 'life sciences', including biology.

The Canada Council has built up an international reputation for the scrupulous independence of its judgment and the competence of its service to its university constituency. subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION (SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES) ACT, 1976 MEASURES RESPECTING ORGANIZATION OF CERTAIN SCIENTIFIC ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak on Bill C-26 respecting the organization of scientific activities of the government of Canada. It is an important subject. I am puzzled why a bill so basic to our way of life and well-being should be smuggled in for consideration at second reading for such a brief period. I know that second reading involves agreement in principle. I suppose the present procedure is a reflection on our peculiar priorities. I
April 22, 1977

will try to be brief in my remarks this afternoon because much of what I wanted to say on the bill has already been said.
Science, of course, is a two-edged sword. It provides us with the good life, it seeks to cure our worst problems and tries to provide us with a good lifestyle. It is the responsibility of the federal government to ensure that our limited resources are put to the best possible use and that we use our resources efficiently and effectively to gain the ends we seek. This is no easy task. Much wisdom and determination is evident in this bill. 1 see before us the potential for a great deal of progress. We shall be led into a new era by science. I do not think we should be misled by the fact that many of the provisions of the bill appear to be technical or administrative changes. The potential effects of the bill are much greater than that.
As has been mentioned several times, we are to have two new granting councils: the natural sciences and engineering research council, which will be involved with the physical sciences, and the social sciences and humanities research council. There is to be an intercouncil co-ordinating committee which will involve both new councils. There is a second major change in the bill. There is to be a change in the mandate of various research organizations answering to the government, namely, the National Research Council, the Canada Council, the Science Council, the Defence Research Board, and the Medical Research Council-the latter being particularly close to my interests.
I should like to touch on three main areas of concern. First I shall raise the role of the federal government in the conduct of scientific research; second, stemming from my background in medicine and pharmaceutical research, the implication for health research contingent upon the proposed enlargement of responsibilities for the Medical Research Council; and, third, the role of private industry in promoting research in this country.
Our government must play a co-ordinating role in science. Without doubt, there is need for a greater co-ordinating role. The federal government has the right to do this, even though traditionally and constitutionally this field has fallen under provincial responsibility. Really, my point relates to the old saying that "he who pays the piper calls the tune". It is a fact that the federal government is the largest single source of money for research activity in this country.
We are responsible for making sure that our research is conducted in the most efficient way, which means that we must get the best results with the lowest expenditure. That, also, means the smallest waste of our resources. In this respect, I feel we ought to put more emphasis than we have in the past on what I call mission-oriented research. We need to make certain that the federal government gives direction in that respect. Such activity ought to be placed in direct contrast to so-called curiosity-oriented research which is done in our halls of ivy, in academic circles and cloistered laboratories. Such research is done purely for the purpose of extending knowledge, and not always with concrete results in mind for the betterment of mankind. In other words, such research brings about little which ordinary people can use.
Scientific Activities of Government
Our work these days must be done in a much broader context and people in research, including those in our universities, must be aware of this. This is an age-old problem. Both kinds of research must be supported. However, in these days, when we are labouring under economic restraint and a restraint of our physical resources, there must be a well defined basis of relevance for all research, particularly basic research.
That brings me to the role of the granting councils of the government. I am thinking of the way in which those councils solicit research or obtain the sort of research this country needs through the use of our centralized information facilities. It is felt that the benefits of the new system will be several. Such work will be done more cheaply and quickly and will lead to more predictable results. That point bears directly on the role of government and is important.
I come now to my second concern, the role of the Medical Research Council. I am thinking of medical research and what it will do for the health of the people of this country. I think this bill has the potential for directing our health research into areas in which we urgently need it. It is not always so. There is a great deal of curiosity-oriented research in the health field. It has been mentioned by several members in this debate, notably by my colleague, the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine), that the MRC needs a new mandate.
While it is a technically simple change as it reads in the bill, it indicates a very significant and fundamental shift in the role of the MRC, a shift which is certainly in line with another program of the Department of National Health and Welfare called "The New Perspective on the Health of Canadians", a program I have mentioned many times, as have other members. Remarkably, only a few words were changed in the Medical Research Council Act, but those words are of enormous significance.
In the past, our main problem has been physical illness. Our least concern has been with preventing illness, promoting positive health, fitness, and so on. We have been too busy trying to cure illness that has already occurred. Therefore, in the act there was very little provision for preventive or public health research. The words "other than public health research" which prevented that will now be dropped. That is long overdue.
This is one of the healthiest nations in the world in terms of medical facilities, treating illness and looking after people who report to us sick. We have the hospitals, nurses, everything we need, yet somehow we still seem to have a great deal of illness. It is peculiar and disappointing for a country of this affluence. This is the direction we need to go in the future. We think we can look after most of our physical illness barring some very necessary breakthroughs in certain diseases such as heart disease and cancer, those which still cause serious illness and the highest rates of death. However, most of our health problems are preventable, social, and in many cases imaginary. Very little has been done in this field.

April 22, 1977
Scientific Activities of Government
As a nation, we may not be very ill but we are not in very good shape. By way of example, and without meaning to be the least bit partisan or personal, I would like to review a study on nutrition that was done last year by the CBC. it was done on federal members of parliament. There were some very interesting results which I would like to quote. First, Conservatives averaged 1416 pounds of excess baggage; New Democrats, 16 pounds-

speechtext:
-Socreds, 30; and the Liberals, although they were the lightest of the heavyweights, still weighed in 13 pounds too much. Second, nine out of ten MPs let their jobs affect their eating habits. That will come as no surprise, especially after lunch. Third, out of an over-all nutrition score of 100, hon. members of this institution failed, with a miserable average score of 42-less than 50 per cent. Fourth, typical of the irresponsible attitude of some MPs toward their eating habits is a comment made by one member who said, "I eat only junk food. I like it."
In comparison to this sorry state of affairs were the comments made by Dr. Zach I. Sabrey, a nutritionist and syndicated columnist. He said doctors-and I strongly agree-are trained and taught only how to treat the sick, not the healthy or disease-free. He stated that, as a result, a recent analysis has determined that about 40 per cent, or $916 million of all hospital care costs in Canada, are spent on the treatment of nutrition-related diseases each year. We know that only a tiny fraction of the training of a medical doctor is on the subject of nutrition. Even more shocking, Dr. Sabrey estimates that the yearly loss of productivity due to premature death from these diseases costs in the order of $4.75 billion. There, for anyone who may feel that health is an optional subject, is the real kicker because to most of us money is very, very important.
We also know the problems associated with other areas, some of which are now receiving some attention and getting some results, such as automobile accidents, the related area of seat-belt use, and lower speeds, smoking, alcohol, drug abuse, the lack of fitness and sport for most of our people related to our Participaction program. There is a very high incidence of psychological illness in this country-over 50 per cent of all illness that is reported. That is a serious problem, one in which we are now just beginning to get correct direction and enough research money to handle it. Many lives and dollars can be saved. However, we will still have to fight this problem in terms of our own attitudes, people in the field and public attitudes resulting in the fact that there is little research in preventive medicine and social sciences and very little public demand for it.
What are some of the fields which have been ignored and on which we should concentrate? Very briefly, programs aimed at particular segments of the over-all population as opposed to individual episodes of sickness; investigation of improved and more cost-benefit effective modes of health care delivery; research in the field of occupational health hazards; research into mental illness associated with environmental and lifestyle;

future-oriented research aimed at anticipating health threats and opportunities; research concerning the long-range influence of environmental health hazards. One could go on indefinitely, Mr. Speaker.
Finally, I would like to touch briefly on something that concerns me very much. This is the role of private industry in promoting research. From my experience-and this is unfortunate-it is certainly very different in other countries, and they have had better results in this respect than Canada. Private industry seems to remain isolated in our Canadian community, for some reason or another. There are many facts associated with this fact and many reasons for it. One, there seems to be a traditional classic attitude in this country, a classic academic elite between the partners of government and universities in terms of doing a certain kind of research.
We set up the National Research Council on that basis, but with the idea that our own government research would be fed into private industry, which would provide Canada with a great industrial base. Well, it did not happen. Goodness knows why. It is probably more because of human factors than any other reason. In fact, we should recognize that fact at this point and realize that we have to take another approach.
In addition, there seems to be an equally strong reaction on the part of private industry in that it does not want to be associated with government and universities. Private industry has developed, particularly with the influx of foreign-owned companies, a branch plant economy. It has developed a great deal of its own research facilities, perhaps not as much as we would like to see. In many cases it prefers to go its own way and not get involved in the trouble of being associated with government regulations, academic fickleness, and all the rest. Government has tried to help industry in many ways in recent years, with limited success, in terms of tax incentives, package programs such as IRD1A, PAIT, PEP, and the rest of the so-called "alphabet soup" programs which in many cases are too inflexible to be useful to industry.
The recent "make or buy" policy means that more government research is farmed out on contract to private companies. However, this does not really expand our research in this country. It certainly does not expand our industrial thrust, because we are really still doing government research, only we have somebody else doing it. So it is a case of shifting work and not expanding our efforts.
[DOT] (M30)
The recent budget attempted to do more. It is a step in the right direction but apparently there is a long way to go. It attempted to do more to help research, particularly in the private sector, through investment tax credits of 5 per cent here in central Canada and higher rates in other regions where, perhaps, it is hoped to attract the companies and research units. This covers both operating and capital expenses in research for the first time in my memory, and it remains to be seen whether this works.
As I said before, we have the problem of being a branch plant economy. A great deal of the research work traditionally
April 22, 1977

has been done in the parent companies, particularly in the United States and Europe, rather than in Canada and it is a problem which still has to be solved. I do not think the position has been particularly helped by some of the things we have done in government, for example, some of the provisions we have made in patent laws have very seriously inhibited research in the Canadian pharmaceutical industry. This is a subject which will certainly come up again in the near future. The idea was all right. It lowered prices to the consumer and presented a good argument on that side, but it certainly did little to stimulate the research industry in this country.
Before 1 conclude, Mr. Speaker, I should like briefly to mention Canadian patents and development-the transfer of responsibility for Canadian Patents and Development Limited from the National Research Council to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. This is a very interesting move and, hopefully, it will have practical results in getting government research work into the hands of industry where it can be used in an effective commercial way for the good of individual Canadian companies as well as for the good of the Canadian economy.
Those are my specific remarks. In conclusion, I should like to say I believe the bill before us is an excellent step in the evolvement of science policy, though a subtle one. I might dwell here on what might appear to be administrative changes-a clean-up bill. This is because I believe these changes have far greater implications for the whole thrust of science policy in Canada than their simple technical nature would suggest. With greater co-ordination of the various councils' granting functions and the sharper definition of the agencies' duties, I think there is great potential for improved efficiency and rationalization of all our resources.
I would like to emphasize once again that this bill only places the potential for progress within our grasp. It is still a very heavy responsibility to take advantage of it and to combine these innovations with a real desire to promote co-ordination and efficiency throughout the whole bureaucratic structure through which they must pass and in which they so often bog down. 1 believe the bill, if it passes, will prove to be a very important catalyst to vigorous activity in all areas of research in Canada and, hopefully, to a healthier use of science and technology by Canadian society as a whole.

Mr. Speaker,
I should like to say a few words about Bill C-26 which has been before the House for a while. We know that not all of the organizations which are being restructured by the bill are in favour of it. Certainly the Canada Council is not. It is no secret that the council is unanimously opposed to the division of its functions, and because such bodies have reservations about the bill we should ask what some of its advantages are. I regret the minister is not here this afternoon, and I trust that in his summation he will address himself to this aspect of the debate.
I should like to use a specific example through which the hon. gentleman might be able to clear up some of the doubt in my mind, as well as in the minds of many British Columbians, regarding the powers the various bodies will have once the reorganization is completed. The question has been raised with the minister, the National Research Council, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Premier of British Columbia, and by the Astrophysical Observatory Committee, a group interested in preserving the function of the existing Dominion Radio-Astrophysical Observatory at White Lake, near Penticton, B.C.
The concern those people feel for this important scientific installation is based on the past performance of the government because they know, as many representatives in this House know, that the Queen Elizabeth Optical Observatory which was to have been built at Mount Kobau in the southern Okanagan, and which was under way at the time of the great Trudeaumania sweep of 1968, was cancelled by the government almost immediately after that victory. Of course, the cancellation of that project had a two-edged pain to it, because there was concern not only among the scientific fraternity but among Canadians who knew that it had been a centennial gift in the name of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth and that the cancellation of it, even on scientific grounds, was inconceivable to many British Columbians.
At a time when one sees, again, a replay of the campaign of 1968 being conducted across the west, this bill presents an opportunity to raise questions about an installation which should have been in place, and would have been in place, serving a role in Canada had there not been a lack of concern for the kind of constitutional monarchy that we are and also for the role of scientific installations in the province of British Columbia.
Therefore, one approaches Bill C-26 with a certain amount of skepticism. I would be interested in knowing, and I am sure the Astrophysical Observatory Committee would be very interested in knowing just which of the bodies that are to be set up by this bill will be responsible for the fate of the Dominion Radio-Astrophysical Observatory. It is amazing that one can still refer to a federal government installation using the adjective "dominion", but the government may get around to

Pension Act
changing that, too. Will it be the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council? Will it be the Science Council of Canada? Or will it still be the National Research Council?
In the past the committee has appealed to the National Research Council and had from them the reply that, given their financial situation, they cannot see their way to spending money to protect the installation so as to guarantee that its functions will not be interfered with in the future. On reading that correspondence, one wonders how enthusiastically the letters were written. If the government had not starved the National Research Council, as it has over the last few years, if the government had not kept a tighter rein on the council's budget than on some other budgets, the NRC might have been able to take more firm and definite action to reduce electrical interference.
I should like to ask the minister a question which I trust will be referred to him. It is this: Should the bill pass, where would the committee place its concern? To whom should it appeal next? I know letters have been written to the minister on this question; indeed I wrote to him myself on April 14, so he is aware of the situation. I do not know whether he is awaiting passage of Bill C-26; but certainly I, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker), and the committee itself would be interested in the minister's response and how he feels about the question.
We would like to know whether reorganizing all these councils for the sciences, humanities and the arts will remove the councils further from political interference, or whether they will suffer the same fate as the CRTC, the CBC and a variety of other councils and agencies. We are wondering whether this is not part and parcel of a series of changes enabling the government to interfere in these jurisdictions far more directly. We are well aware of the orders that were given to the CRTC, about which I am sure many Canadians are concerned.
The hon. member who preceded me so eloquently described this bill as "subtle". From Liberal governments that have been in power since 1968 we have come to learn about the subtlety of government and its bills. I hope that when the minister replies and winds up the debate he will reassure us that he will give the observatory committee his thoughts regarding their appeal and, given the passage of this bill, that he will have some advice for them.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that we agreed to the principle of the bill on second reading, I am glad to say we still have no quarrel with the passage of the bill which, as we indicated before, will provide for a deputy chairman of the Pension Review Board in order to allow for double sittings and, hopefully, increase the adjudication process by adding two ad hoc members. We trust this will clear up the backlog of applications which have been waiting for too long. I do not intend to speak long on this bill; I wish merely to raise a couple of points. I should like to review from the report "Veterans Canada" the function of the Pension Review Board, which at page 32 is described as follows:
The board has final authority to determine any questions of law or fact as to whether a person is entitled to an award under the Pension Act and the amount of any such award. The function of the board is purely judicial as the administration of the Pension Act is the responsibility of the Canadian Pension Commission. The decision of the board is final and binding for all purposes of the act. It is also authorized to entertain any request for an interpretation of the Pension Act made by the commission, the chief pensions advocate or any veterans organization incorporated by or under any act of the parliament of Canada.
Another section of the report reads as follows:
The board holds of paramount importance its responsibility to consider all requests for the interpretation of any provisions of the Pension Act. The question of interpretation is made the subject of hearing before all members of the board when the commission, the bureau of pensions advocates, and all veterans' organizations are invited to appear. The subject matter is fully aired at the hearing before the issue is determined by the board.
This is pretty straightforward, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is long past the time when consideration should be given to, and some flexibility shown in, the adjudication of pensions. Since many veterans are getting older and are unable to get the evidence to back up their claim that they were injured during the war, it has now come to the point where they are being forsaken. This brings up the question of benefit of the doubt, a matter which is not given the consideration that it merits.
I should like to put before the House a case that was brought to my attention of a lady whose husband died having served in the First World War for a year between 1914 and 1917. That is not disputed. The case came to my attention because this poor veteran died in 1974, and his widow, who cannot manage financially, is looking for a widow's pension. We went through the various stages and ended up with some compassionate award that might be granted to her because of the fact the veteran was not treated properly, in my opinion, or his case was not adjudicated properly.
April 22, 1977

Going back to the stated case, which is another reason why there is such a backlog of pensions, the many hundreds of pages of a stated case must be prepared in duplicate or in triplicate. Yet we cannot seem to find that humane humanist to adjudicate a case with the veteran in mind and the conditions. In 1914 this veteran was 18'/2 years old. He lost his hearing on May 21, 1915, and his sight and speech, as a result of shellfire shock. He recovered his sight almost at once, and he recovered his speech after three days. He still suffered from weakness and many effects that certainly support the fact that he was injured and the fact that he suffered continuously until his death in 1974.
He was in hospital with a 25 per cent disability. It was generally acknowledged that he was gassed; a trench fell in on him, and every type of thing happened that justified a request for a pension. It ended up with a decision of the then board, or commission which granted him a gratuity of $25, as provided for in an approved minute of Privy Council of June 3, 1916. He suffered all along. There are doctors' certificates to the fact that he suffered many years since 1916.
We are at the stage now where on Monday morning the widow will appear before the Pension Review Board. I was asked to appear on her behalf. I cannot go because this bill will be before us. I am trying to impress on the House and the minister that this is the type of case which is hanging around and costing the taxpayers thousands of dollars. If we cost it out, the process from the application to the appeal until the adjudication-in most cases they are turned down-we will find we would be better off and would be serving the veterans in a more humane way if they were granted a pension before they die feeling that Canada has forsaken them after the service they gave.
This is one of the things that should be considered. We must have a review of the legislation. This is why I asked for a review of all phases of the Veterans Act back in March of this year. I hope the minister, who is always saying he is considering everything, will review cases like this. There are hundreds of cases like this where we could repay veterans and fulfil the commitments made to them many years ago.
Evidently all the veterans' organizations agree with this. Evidently everybody but the minister agrees with it. In the managerial advisory boards we have it is just a matter of procrastination. First World War veterans are now over 80 years old, and Second World War veterans are over 60 years old. We still do not have finality to the treatment of veterans, even with all the studies that have been made over the years.
We made a serious error when we passed Bill C-92 respecting the prisoners of war compensation act. I mention the fact that First World War veterans were not included. I mention the fact that there are only 200 of them left. I mention the fact that it would only cost $200,000, and this would gradually phase out over the next few years. We forgot another important group-the escapees and the evaders-who certainly suffered; in a lot of cases more than those who were incarcerated.
Pension Act
A very strong letter from the Royal Air Force Escapee Society points out the many inequities which exist. It also points out some of the points the officials made in the Department of Veterans Affairs. For example, the deputy minister indicated that the new legislation would follow studies made by Dr. J. Douglas Hermann, of the former European POWs, as a result of the obvious inequities in the pensions for Hong Kong veterans. As for world war POWs, escapees and evaders, the deputy minister said:
I don't feel there is necessarily any justification for additional benefits. No studies have been carried out on these people and there are no future benefits planned for them.
If no studies were carried out, why were they not carried out? The association gives examples of the suffering that some of these escapees had. They did everything in their power to help fight the enemy even when in danger. There were threats by the Luftwaffe and the German army. Fifty of the Commonwealth flyers who took part in the "great escape" from Stalag Luft-111, Germany, were murdered by the Gestapo. They were always under the threat of being murdered. They did everything possible to evade. They suffered just as much in some cases as any veteran who was incarcerated. At this late date, I ask that some humane consideration be given to them. I hope the minister will consider this request, if he takes the time to read my speech.

I want to get the Pension Review Board built up with strength so that it can adjudicate cases more quickly and efficiently, and clean up the backlog of some 3,000 cases which still remain. The fact that these veterans sacrificed their lives should be considered with a much more humanist Canadian spirit.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) who has just spoken, I want to express our pleasure at having an opportunity to support Bill C-11, which

April 22, 1977
Pension Act
is now at third reading. Its purpose is to strengthen the Pension Review Board both by providing for a deputy chairman and by providing for additional members so that that board can more expeditiously do the work that is given to it. The Pension Review Board, as hon. members are aware, is a body completely separate from the Canadian Pension Commission to which applications for pensions which have been denied by that commission can be referred for further review. It is significant that the Pension Review Board does alter the decision made by the Canadian Pension Commission in respect of between 30 per cent and 35 per cent of the cases that are sent up to the Pension Review Board. In the view of some of us this makes it obvious that it was a good decision we made a number of years ago following study of the report of the Woods commission. I refer to the decision to establish a pension review board. We are pleased to indicate our support for this bill, as we did at second reading and in the standing committee, and I hope that within not many minutes the bill will have been passed by this House.
Like the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, however, I feel that when the subject of veterans affairs comes up it ought to be said strongly, and with as much of a note of appeal to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), and to the government as we can muster, that there are matters of unfinished business that still require attention.
I have no hesitation in saying that for a few years, from about 1970 to 1974, we made quite a few improvements in veterans legislation but then things seemed to taper off. The only improvement that we have had in this majority parliament, compared with some significant improvements that were won during the minority parliament, is the passing of the bill to provide prisoners of war compensation for those who were prisoners of war in Europe and improvements in the prisoners of war compensation for those who were prisoners of war in Hong Kong. That was good legislation, but the rate of improvement in veterans legislation has declined greatly since the early years of this decade.
Some people might say everything has been fixed up. It is not so, Mr. Speaker. There are some items of unfinished business that some of us think are very serious. There is an understandable tendency on the part of veterans to feel that, because we are getting more and more decades away from the wars in which they took part, they are being forgotten.
It is in more than just a formal sense that I rise for these few minutes, as my colleague from Newfoundland has done, to appeal to the Minister of Veterans Affairs to put even more fight into his efforts on behalf of the veterans. If I wanted to disagree slightly with my colleague-and it is not often that I do, as we often say the same thing-I would question one thing he said a moment ago. He said that everybody but the Minister of Veterans Affairs agreed with the particular appeal he was making. I will go further. I will say the Minister of Veterans Affairs also agrees, but he is in trouble with some of those in the cabinet, such as the Minister of Finance (Mr. 
Macdonald), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who seem to know nothing but restraint.
We are talking about World War I veterans who are over 80 years of age. We are talking about widows in the same bracket. We are talking about World War II veterans who are in their sixties and are having a tough time. To tell them that restraint is the order of the day and ask them to wait 10 or 20 years until things improve is not a proper response on the part of parliament or the government.
I plead for attention to the items of unfinished business, something like the attention we were getting when we were studying the Woods report and during the months in which the government was in a minority position. The previous speaker referred to some of those items, and he said I would repeat them. He is perfectly right.
I have already mentioned the bill of last year regarding the prisoners of war pension. It is a shame it took so many years to win that bill, but it was good that we won it. Mr. Speaker, it is still wrong that we did not include in the bill, or that the government did not include in the bill, as the committee recommended, prisoners of war from World War I. There are only 200 of them still alive, so the cost would be minuscule compared with the way money is thrown around in this place. It is not good enough to say that can be considered after the period of restraint is over. When the period of restraint is over, things will be over for them as well. The same goes for the escapers and evaders in World War II; they should have been included in the bill passed last year. Incidentally, that was the recommendation both of Dr. Hermann, who brought in the report, and of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
The minister keeps indicating his sympathy with respect to our position on those matters, and I believe him. I think the trouble is not in his heart or soul; his trouble is with those so-and-so's he has to get along with in cabinet. I plead for action on those two issues with respect to the bill we passed last year.
Another issue that we raise fairly often which I think still requires attention is the gap that has developed between the rate of a 100 per cent disability pension and the composite figure in the public service that was accepted as a norm a few years ago. At that time the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs recommended that, a composite figure for the public service having been established as a norm for 100 per cent disability pension, that should continue to be the norm. As the composite rate in the public service went up, so the rate of the 100 per cent disability should go up, indeed, by the same number of dollars. But the government pegged it to the rise in the consumer price index. The result is that now there is a gap of more than $500 per year between the rate of the 100 per cent disability pension and the composite rate in the five groups in the public service that were taken for that purpose. That is a piece of unfinished business that ought to be dealt with by this parliament, which means that the Minister of Veterans Affairs should be persuaded to get cabinet to let him bring in a bill amending that piece of legislation.

Another matter that is of serious concern, and is still a shortcoming of which parliament cannot be proud, is the way we cut off the widows of veterans from any pension as of right if the veteran's pension was less than 48 per cent. We have fought about this so often and recited the story so often that I am sure every one must know how it works. If a veteran is on a disability pension of 48 per cent or more and dies, his widow gets, as a right, without any question, the full widow's pension, which is 75 per cent of a 100 per cent disability pension. If the veteran's pension was below 48 per cent-if it was 47 per cent, 46 per cent or 45 per cent-she gets nothing.
There are many cases where there are also other benefits that the veteran was getting but which die with him. She can go on various forms of welfare. She can get the welfare program of the department which is an allowance for widows under the War Veterans Allowance Act. It is a fact of life however, that persons, civilians or veterans, veterans or widows, feel a lot different about something that comes as a matter of right and something to which there is the stigma of welfare or a means test attached.
We have argued, and we have had excellent recommendations along those lines, that at the very least there should be pro rata pensions for widows in those cases. If the veteran's pension was less than 48 per cent, the widow should get at least a proportion of the pension. This has been recommended by such outstanding persons as Mr. Justice Mervyn Woods who brought in the Woods report a few years ago which recommended action, by Dr. J. D. Hermann in his report on prisoners of war, and by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs several times. I believe the Minister of Veterans Affairs also thinks it should be done, and I am pretty well satisfied that the bureaucrats in his department-there are pretty good bureaucrats in that department-want this to be done. Where is the block? Where is the trouble? It is in the cabinet. It is the President of the Treasury Board, it is the Minister of Finance, it is the Prime Minister himself, I suspect, who say "No, we cannot put any more money into veterans affairs; we have done enough."
Sir, these are pressing problems that should be met and resolved. 1 am taking this opportunity this afternoon, not just in a formal way, not just because veterans affairs are before us, but to plead with the minister that he deal with these matters at an early date. I offer no complaint at his absence. He has one of the better attendance records in the House of any member of cabinet. He is here night after night, and I am sure his absence this afternoon is for a very good reason. I also
Pension Act
know he will read this debate, and I hope he will pay close attention to it.
I press also-and this is in line with something the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe just said-that we do some more thinking about the position of older veterans. Once veterans are past the age of 60, once they are in their seventies or eighties, are we not spending an awful lot of money needlessly on the red tape and investigation of their means, health, and all the rest of it? Surely a time comes when instead of denying veterans their rights because they cannot meet certain tests, or instead of giving them a war veterans allowance with a means test attached, it is right for these veterans and their widows that we establish a guaranteed income. As the previous speaker said, it would save a lot of costs of one kind or another, and certainly it would be more fair.
I welcome this opportunity and I say my word of thanks to Your Honour. As a matter of fact if you had taken the trouble to read the bill-and maybe you did-you would wonder how the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe and I could drag in the whole gamut of veterans affairs under a little bill to increase the size of the Pension Review Board. But you are very decent and I am glad you allowed us to do it. I hope the minister will read the speeches that have been made this afternoon and will realize it is not good enough to trade on the improvements that were made for veterans over a number of years.
We have not done enough lately. We should be doing something now, and I hope that attention will be given to the important issues we have placed on the record this afternoon.
