Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to speak on this bill, but it is not very often that anything is presented in the House in the form of a bill on veterans affairs which would give us an opportunity to speak on this subject. Although this bill is just a housekeeping bill and something that the cabinet could have done by order in council without bringing in legislation before the House, I think also there are too many areas in which the cabinet does act on its own, such as restrictions on the amounts of money that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) can use for veterans. I think it is a good thing that at least we have a bill such as this which gives us the opportunity to speak on matters concerning veterans.
I apologize to be speaking only on third reading of the bill, but I could not speak on the previous stages of the bill. I cannot be as charitable regarding this bill as was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and I hope that this legislation will not mean there will be more of the same from the Pension Review Board. What the bill does is to increase the length of service of the members of the board from five to ten years. It gives them a chance to bring in some ad hoc members or to increase their staff when they deem it necessary, and it allows them to have a vice chairman, and so on. But if it means more of the same, then I am not really too much in favour of this bill because, as the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) said, what is

April 22, 1977
Pension Act
necessary is to clean up the backlog and deal with those veterans who have made their plea for pensions. There are some 3,000 of them, and we need to do something for them.
I am also somewhat concerned about some of the findings of the Pension Review Board, having had an opportunity to appear before them in the case of a veteran and having had an opportunity to review what happened in his case over the years in his attempts to obtain some recognition of his need for a pension. It appears to me that the Pension Review Board has acted to protect in particular the interests of the doctors in the armed forces, especially in the case of my constituent who is a very conscientious man. He has served in the armed forces for a long period of time, starting early in the second world war. Actually he joined up under age. On being found out, he was discharged, but then immediately upon coming of age he joined up again. He served in the armed forces through the latter part of the second world war and in peace time. He has a very good service record, so he cannot be faulted for that.
During his service he was at times sick and in distress, and it appears to me that quite often he was given shocking treatment. I would even accuse the armed forces of having diagnosed this case improperly. At one time he was posted to a restricted area of service improperly because people with medical problems were not supposed to go there. Whilst there he could not receive the type of treatment he needed, nor was his illness correctly diagnosed. Finally, after years of service and after he left the armed forces, he received the proper treatment for his ailment. He had regional ileitis, and it was properly treated, but only after years and years of treatment in the armed forces.
The Review Board always says new evidence has to be brought in, but I do not think it is new evidence; it is a new look, because in my opinion the board does not take into consideration the reports of civilian doctors. In my opinion this veteran was given shocking treatment in the armed services, and this is not really being given proper consideration. Factually erroneous medical reports are continually being cited to justify denying him a pension.
I think this Chamber is the highest court in the land, much higher than the review board, and I feel it is my duty to raise this matter because of the treatment the review board has given this person. The board is using old and outdated texts on regional ileitis. The most recent research has shown that this disease begins in early teenage years and progresses more rapidly in later years. It also has shown that it can be aggravated by the very type of treatment this veteran received during his time in the armed forces. I do not believe these areas are being examined.
As I said before, all the records of this individual show that he was a very good worker, that he was very conscientious, and that he made every effort to avoid sick leave.
Even though this bill is a housekeeping bill, I cannot get really too excited about supporting it unless we are going to get something better from the review board. If it is just going

to be the maintenance of the status quo, if we are just going to give the review board this and that, not bring the backlog down, not really take a good objective look at cases like this, and if we just refer to one authoritative report which was put in by an armed forces doctor, I really cannot get too excited about supporting the bill.
As I said before, there are many things happening in the Department of Veterans Affairs. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that these things happen because of internal decisions of the cabinet. I certainly hope that in the interests of veterans the Minister of Veterans Affairs is being supported by the cabinet. I hope the cabinet realizes that perhaps veterans have not had the opportunity to file for pensions or that perhaps they have been too proud. I hope also that the cabinet realizes that some ailments are not known at the time veterans leave the armed forces and that veterans should be given another opportunity to make application. It is unfortunate when the minister has to say to the Pension Review Board that sufficient funds for veterans are not available.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for this opportunity to say these few words, and I hope that in future veterans will get a much better deal from the Pension Review Board.

speakeroldname: Hon. Len Marchand (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
that Bill C-48, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise, to move second reading of Bill C-48, which proposes certain changes to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, and the Small Businesses Loans Act. As Minister of State for Small Business, I have, of course, a very special interest in the Small Businesses Loans Act. I think it appropriate, however, that I should also speak to the changes recommended in the acts for farmers and Fishermen. The three acts have very similar objectives and provisions and they have always been regarded as companion programs.
These programs have been in existence for many years, and I expect that most hon. members will be quite familiar with them. It will be recalled that the purpose of the legislation is to facilitate the availability of intermediate term credit to farmers, fishermen, and small businessmen. Under the legislation the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is authorized to guarantee loans made by chartered banks and other designated lenders for a wide range of capital improvement purposes, subject to certain conditions being met.
This legislation will expire on June 30 of this year unless extended by parliament, and one of the purposes of Bill C-48 is to seek a continuation of it for another three years. Other changes are also being recommended with a view to keeping the programs abreast of economic trends and developments. However, before discussing provisions of the bill in detail it
Improvement Loans
might be helpful if I said a few words about these programs in more general terms.
An important feature of all three is that loans can be made without prior approval of the minister. This arrangement greatly facilitates the speed with which loan applications can be processed, and is intended to ensure that the borrower's needs are dealt with efficiently and expeditiously.
During my consultations with members of the small business community all over the country, one of the most frequently heard complaints has been that when business has to deal with government, the turn-around time on a decision is too long for a small operator's needs. Under this program he can get the Financing he requires without undue delay.
At the same time a loan must be made in accordance with specified criteria if it is to be eligible for a guarantee. These requirements include the maximum amount of a loan, the purpose of the loan, its maximum term security, the minimum investment by the borrower in the project for which a loan is sought, and the maximum rate of interest which can be charged. Finally, in all cases lenders are expected to use responsible business judgment in assessing applications.
I should like to speak now about some of the features specific to the Small Businesses Loans Act. I propose to deal with this program First because, though not the oldest or the largest of the three, it has been growing the most rapidly and I believe it offers considerable additional scope as an instrument for assisting small businesses.
The Small Businesses Loans Act came into effect in 1961 for a three-year period, and has been extended and amended from time to time since then. In order to qualify for a loan an enterprise must, at present, have an annual gross revenue not exceeding $1 million and be engaged in one of the following forms of business activity: manufacturing, retail or wholesale trade, provision of services, construction, transportation, or communications. Loans purposes include the purchase of fixed or moveable equipment, the purchase, improvement or renovation of premises, and the purchase of land necessary for the operation of a business. The maximum individual loan limit is currently $50,000, and the maximum repayment period is ten years.
From its inception to the end of 1976, over 43,000 loans had been made under this act for a total of about $480 million. Lending volume since 1970 has risen continually from year to year and there was a particularly sharp increase in 1975 to $78 million, which was more than double the 1974 level. On the basis of figures released yesterday by the Department of Finance, 1976 registered a further growth to about $81 million.
As to changes proposed in this program, Bill C-48 recommends an extension for a further three years to June, 1980. An important amendment is also proposed in the individual lending limit, which would be raised from $50,000 to $75,000. The coverage of the small business community would also be enlarged by broadening the eligibility criteria under the act. In future a business would qualify for assistance if its annual

April 22, 1977
Improvement Loans
gross revenue were as high as $1.5 million, an increase of $500,000 from the present limit of $1 million. This would have the effect of making the program more available to the retail sector where a relatively small operation can easily go above $1 million in annual sales.
Finally, the aggregate amount of loans which would be eligible for the guarantee in the proposed three-year lending period would be set at $600 million. There would be only one lending pool applicable to all lenders, instead of, as is presently the case, separate limits for chartered banks and Alberta treasury branches and for other designated lenders such as credit unions and caisses populaires. A single pool would not affect the government's potential exposure and would have the advantage of being a more flexible arrangement.
The figure of $600 million represents a substantial increase over the limit currently in effect, which is $350 million for the three years ending in June, 1977. The increase is necessary in light of the expected increased volume of lending which will result from the changes I have just mentioned, and from the planned adjustment of the rates lenders will be allowed to charge. I will discuss this matter in more detail later in my remarks. At this point 1 would note merely that the present interest rate formula could be changed by regulation under the powers in the existing statute. No amendment to the legislation would be necessary. I should also note it would be the intention to apply a new formula to all three programs, not just to the program under the Small Businesses Loans Act.
The oldest of the three programs is the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which was established in 1944. Eligible loan purposes include the purchase of farm implements, buildings, equipment or livestock, the purchase of additional land, and the repair or improvement of assets used in farming enterprises. As in the case of the Small Businesses Loans Act, the maximum individual loan limit is currently $50,000. The maximum repayment period is also ten years, except in the case of land purchases, where it is 15 years.
The Farm Improvement Loans Act has played an important role in assisting the development of Canadian agriculture, as is attested to by the lending activity it has helped to generate. From its inception to the end of 1976, over 1,750,000 loans were made under the act, totalling about $3.5 billion. Loans in 1976, on the basis of figures released yesterday, were in the order of $160 million.
The proposed changes in the Farm Improvement Loans Act are similar to those recommended for the Small Businesses Loans Act. The program will be extended for three years to June 30, 1980, and the individual lending limit would be increased from $50,000 to $75,000. The aggregate lending limit for the proposed new period would be set at $1.55 billion, somewhat higher than the limit for the current three-year period of $1.4 billion. As in the case of the Small Businesses Loans Act, separate limits for banks and for other designated lenders would be replaced by a single pool applicable to all lenders.
The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act was introduced in 1955 and has since been amended as necessary. The purpose

for which loans can be made now includes the purchase, construction, or repair of fishing vessels and fishing equipment, and the development of shore installations such as piers, wharves and boat houses, including equipment which is used with them. The maximum individual loan limit is $50,000 and the maximum repayment period is ten years.
Lending under this program reached a record level of $12 million in the loan year 1975-76. On the basis of figures released yesterday, which record lending activity in the nine months to January 1, the expected volume in the current loan year, though down somewhat, will still be of the order of $10.5 million.
As in the case of the amendments proposed to programs for farmers and small business people, the lending period under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act would be extended for a further three years and the individual lending limit increased to $75,000. The limit on loans subject to guarantee in the new three-year period would be $80 million. As for the other two programs, there would be only one lending pool, instead of two.
These proposed changes respond to representations received during a recently completed review of the legislation. The broad consensus of views received was that the acts can continue to play a useful role in helping to ensure the availability of intermediate term credit and that they should be extended and updated. There was, however, one major concern expressed. This concern is that the interest rates which lenders are permitted to charge on loans have not always been high enough to ensure a flow of credit fully responsive to demand. It has been a consistent theme when I have listened to representations from small business people wherever I have gone in Canada. They have told me "Our problem is not with interest rates. We know we are in a different position when looking for financing than are the banks' bigger customers, the large firms". "What we need," these business people have told me, "is for the money to be available to us in the first place. If Financing is available, interest rates are a secondary consideration."
Under authority provided in the legislation, rates of interest for these programs are set by order in council in accordance with a formula based on government bond yields. While the formula worked quite satisfactorily for some time following its introduction in 1968, this has been less true in recent years, and there have been occasions when it was well below chartered bank prime. As hon. members are aware, the prim? rate is the lowest rate at which banks are prepared to make funds available to their most creditworthy customers.
In circumstances where the prime rate and the formula rate have diverged rather widely, there has understandably been some reluctance on the part of lenders to participate as fully in the programs as would be desirable. The consensus of views received is that the rate in future should be based on back prime with some margin added to reflect administrative costs.
April 22, 1977

I should say that this particular formula is used by the provinces in their direct lending programs.
In the light of these representations the government has been giving careful consideration to a revision of the formula for the three acts with a view to working out an alternative arrangement which would increase the programs' utilization and effectiveness, while still ensuring that costs to the borrowers are not excessive. It is expected that an examination of the interest rate question will be concluded with lenders within the near future. As I mentioned earlier, any new formula would be put into effect by changing the regulations for the programs.
The suggested increase in the individual lending limit from $50,000 to $75,000, together with the proposed modification of eligibility criteria should significantly enlarge the scope, flexibility, and effectiveness of these programs. The recommended aggregate lending limits reflect the expected impact of these changes, as well as the expectation of much higher lending activity which should flow from a revision of the interest rate arrangements. The changes proposed will, I believe, ensure that these programs will make an enhanced contribution toward meeting the capital requirements of small business, farmers and fishermen.
The Small Businesses Loans Act amendments also reflect closely the requirements of small business people as I have heard them in meetings with small entrepreneurs from St. John's to Victoria. I am sure that they will result in a brighter financial picture for many small business operators all over the country.
I recommend this bill to the House. I hope we can get it into committee as soon as possible where there will be more far-reaching discussion.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the initiative of the minister responsible for small business in Bill C-48 to make some amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act to help small businessmen in Canada. They certainly need assistance in the kind of economy we are facing today.
I commend the minister for the initiatives of raising the loan limit from $50,000 to $75,000 and the eligibility requirement from an annual gross revenue of $1 million to $1,500,000. This takes into account the realities of inflation today and the problems that small businessmen are having in gaining working capital.
Despite these initiatives there are still some fundamental problems facing small businessmen to which the government has not addressed itself in a meaningful way. I think, for example, of what is happening to the power of independent small businessmen in our economy as we move more and more toward domination of the major market sectors by large corporations that are in a monopoly or oligopoly position.
1 think, for example, of the 1971 census which showed out of
153,000	non-financial corporations in Canada, only a mere 626 of these accounted for 63 per cent of all total business
Improvement Loans
assets, 58 per cent of total profits, and paid only 46 per cent of corporate income taxes. This shows that our economy is being dominated by a few relatively large business corporations. The principle of competition is seriously undermined as these large companies are able to corner the market in terms of supplies they sell to small businesses and also in terms of products sold to consumers.
These large corporations have an unfair competitive advantage over the small businessman. When we look at the financing in the various budgets brought forward by this government, we have to conclude that tax measures favour the large business over the small business. Indeed the kinds of corporate tax concessions provided since the government of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been in office have amounted to some $6 billion, but only a fraction of that has gone to small business.
Small business is a tremendously important sector of our economy, employing about 60 per cent of Canadian workers. When we look at the problems we are facing today we see only token gestures on the part of the government in helping out small businessmen. We find, for example, that small businessmen, despite the kind of legislation we have before us, still have great difficulty in obtaining credit. Banks are more often willing to make loans to larger business institutions or foreign businesses than they are to small independent Canadian concerns. Even though the minister has raised the limit of the loan the government will guarantee, he has really not addressed himself to encouraging the banks to make these loans readily available.
The small businessmen I talk to invariably complain about the difficulty of even getting bank managers interested in providing loans to them under the act. In most cases the private banks are not enthusiastic about making loans to small businessmen under this legislation, and it seems to me that unless we go further by introducing, for example, an amendment to the banking legislation making it mandatory for the banks to lend a certain percentage of their loan funds to small business under the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act, or similar provisions, businessmen will still be running into the problem of finding banks reluctant to give them loans. As 1 say, the banks are much more interested in making loans to large corporations which will borrow larger sums from which the return in the form of interest will be higher.
The other difficulty lies with the interest rate itself. Small businessmen are always strapped for working capital. Take the case of a merchant engaged in the clothing business, for example, who needs a cash flow of between $50,000 and $100,000 to purchase his stock for the season. The burden placed on him when he has to borrow money at current interest rates ranging anywhere from 10 to 12 per cent or even higher is a tremendous one, yet somehow the bank loan must be repaid out of the earnings he makes through sales. It would be far more significant if the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) could convince the government to bring
80012 33

April 22, 1977
West Indies
in legislation ensuring a preferential loan rate to small business-not just a voluntary rate on the part of the banks but a mandatory one. This would mean a great deal more than merely raising the loan ceiling.
I notice that, according to a recent survey by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, the most significant problems facing small businessmen today are financing and interest rates. It would be far more beneficial if the government were to do something about bringing down high interest rates as they affect small business, in addition to obliging the banks to be more responsive when lending money out to small business.
Another complaint of small businesses is the amount of regulation and red tape they face in filling out forms for Statistics Canada and other government agencies. I ask the minister responsible for small business to move expeditiously to reduce the number of forms small businesses are obliged to fill out. After all, these firms do not usually have a large staff of accountants and others who can do this work. Often it is the businessman himself who must spend long and weary hours filling out the forms which are demanded. A reduction can be made in the type of information which is sought. Too often there is duplication, and too much detail is demanded.
In the long run, though, it seems to me that to create a healthy environment for small business we must challenge the growing monopoly power of a few of the larger businesses in Canada which will corner the market and sell goods below cost to force smaller competitors out of business. If we are to maintain a healthy small business community the government must begin seriously to restrict monopolistic practices of this kind. In conclusion, 1 commend the government for the initiative it has shown in raising the lending limits, but I ask the minister and his colleagues to consider seriously bringing in a provision to reduce interest rates applicable to small business and to restrict monopoly practices which are taking place to the detriment of thousands of small businesses, which are really the backbone of our economy.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words on the motion moved by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) in regard to establishing a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons to examine the advisability of taking an initiative concerning British West Indies possessions, and specifically the Turks and Caicos Islands. As with most issues which may, at first glance, appear straightforward in their implications and readily analyzable in terms of cause and effect, the present discussion, upon closer study, reveals complex and interlocking social, political, and economic problems.
Although the proposal that Canada have a small portion of its sovereign territory south of the snow line seems an attractive one in view of our winters, 1 submit that an analysis of the facts will reveal many overriding drawbacks to this seemingly congenial idea.
It should be explained first that there are ten separate non-independent British states in the Commonwealth Caribbean, five of which have "Associated State" status and five of which are Crown Colonies. The Associated States at present have complete internal self-government but rely upon Great Britain for the conduct of defence and foreign relations. The five Crown Colonies are more directly under British administration, and range in population from the British Virgin Islands, which number just over 5,000 persons, to Belize, formerly British Honduras, which has approximately 135,000 people. In most of the Associated States there appears to be a general desire to move to independence soon, an ambition which is very much in keeping with the climate of international opinion as manifested by the recommendations of the United Nations Special Committee on Dependent Territories.
Canadian development assistance is important in the area and has contributed significantly to the development programs
(Mr. Symes.]
April 22, 1977

of the independent islands. It is also a region of the world to which many Canadians are attracted for their vacations, and it is perhaps partly as a result of these experiences that there is such a widespread interest in the welfare of the region. The Canadian "profile" tends to be a high one, particularly in the smaller islands of the Windwards and Leewards, a fact that in itself places upon us the onus to act responsibly and to employ particular discretion in considering actions which might have an upsetting effect in the Caribbean. An action undertaken by Canada without much careful thought as to its consequences could have a profoundly disruptive impact on the small countries of the region. Our commitment to continue assisting the Commonwealth Caribbean-and especially the disadvantaged islands in the region-remains strong. This is surely the proper way to proceed, rather than to inject ourselves physically into the midst of a region which is developing its own institutions.
It might be of interest to hon. members if I were to review briefly the nature of Canadian assistance in the Commonwealth Caribbean since the inception of our program in 1958. In that year the West Indies Federation became the first area outside the Colombo Plan to receive Canadian development assistance. After the dissolution of the Federation, initial grants were continued and expanded on an individual island basis with the main emphasis on education.
From 1966 onwards there was a considerable expansion of the Canadian aid program. It was agreed at the Commonwealth Caribbean-Canada Conference of 1966 that the level of Canadian assistance over the next five years would be $75 million, plus an additional $5 million for the University of the West Indies. Tourism was identified as a key sector which would stimulate self-sustained economic growth in the region, and Canada thus extended her assistance to the development of airports. In addition, water supply projects were undertaken; further investment was made in education; and Canada assisted in the strengthening of capabilities in agriculture, particularly through the agricultural development fund of the Caribbean Development Bank of which Canada was a founding member. In fact total Canadian assistance for the five-year period exceeded earlier undertakings and totalled more than $100 million. Since that time Canadian development assistance in the Commonwealth Caribbean has increased substantially to a five year total of about $150 million.
Future Canadian assistance to the region as a whole is under study but it can be said that the major problems in the area- unemployment and income distribution-will receive particular attention, as will regional approaches to economic co-operation and the development of common services in education and transportation particularly in the Leeward and Windward Islands. Our aid program will also seek to encourage integrated agricultural development and will concentrate on low income territories. Although, however, by comparison with some other islands in the area, their per capita income is somewhat higher, consideration is presently being given to the provision of limited and ad hoc amounts of assistance to the British Virgin Islands, the Turks and Caicos Islands and the Cayman Islands to be used for the purchase of small equip-
West Indies
ment related to their local developmental projects and needs and scholarships for study in Canada. This is a token of Canadian interest although the British have, of course, the primary economic as well as the full constitutional responsibility for these territories.
Canadian co-operation with the Caribbean does not take place only through aid programs. There is also significant co-operation at the business level. I am aware of several instances where Canadian companies, in co-operation with Caribbean businessmen, have established joint ventures whereby there has been a transfer to the Caribbean of know-how and technology, and savings for the Caribbean in terms of hard currency. This is a most fruitful sort of co-operation and is welcomed by the Caribbean governments.
Through the holidays of Canadian tourists in the Caribbean, through the immigration of Caribbean peoples to Canada, through business, academic and governmental contacts, the Canadian and Caribbean peoples have come to know each other very well and we have succeeded, I think, in establishing relationships of equality. Without in any way being complacent, I think it is fair to say that our relationship with the Commonwealth Caribbean is a good one, devoid of the grinding of axes.
A major problem in the small Commonwealth Caribbean countries is the administration of separate local government units, with the civil service necessary to support them. Most of the Associated States are confronted by the problem of recurrent budgetary deficits incurred in the attempt to maintain minimum acceptable levels of government services. Except for Belize, which is a special case, the dependent territories are smaller than the Associated States, and need outside assistance which the British government provides. For this reason, many of these non-independent states have been working to increase the extent of regional co-operation and to rationalize as much as possible the regional infra-structure.
An example of this has been the Caribbean Community and Common Market-CARICOM-which, in addition to the independent Caribbean states, includes all five of the British Associated States together with the independent territories of Montserrat and Belize. Although primarily an economic grouping, committed to the adoption of a common external tariff, the Caribbean Community also makes provision for consultation on subjects such as regional air and sea transportation and the administration of development assistance programs. CARICOM is an organization which is generally supported by Canada. We hope it will serve to broaden the areas of co-operation between the individual states of the region. It would seriously weaken the prospects for greater Caribbean unity if Canada were to appear to entertain seriously the prospect of detaching some of these countries from their Commonwealth Caribbean associations and integrating them into the Canadian system.
Now I ask members to try to envisage the situation which would result if Canada were to accept into Confederation a
80012-33Vi

April 22, 1977
West Indies
given island of the region, say the Turks and Caicos with a population of about 7,000 people. Presumably, through rapid transfers from the Canadian Treasury to the island, the standard of living on that island would rise dramatically, but a large influx of Canadians could impose a very severe strain on the social fabric and culture of these small territories. Within a comparatively short period of time this new piece of Canadian territory would be clearly marked off from its neighbours. Intolerable pressures would then be generated on the governments of nearby islands, by the peoples of those islands clamouring for services of the same high standard as that prevailing in the Canadianized island. Needless to say, the governments could not possibly afford to meet the expectations thus created.
The Caribbean already suffers, to a significant degree, from the unsettling effects of tourism. Hon. members will know that in most of the Caribbean, Canadian tourists are warmly welcomed and treated with consideration and friendliness. However, tourists can sometimes, without so intending, create by their very presence among the peoples of the Caribbean a desire for North American standards of living which the economies of these islands cannot begin to support. How much more difficult the situation would be if there were also an integral, if detached, part of Canada with standards so high that islands in the area could not begin to meet them. How would we rectify the dis-equilibrium which we would have introduced? How would we react if in island after island the pressures on the governments became too great for them to bear? How would we answer the independent states of the region which might argue that Canada would have created for itself a moral obligation to ensure that these independent states were in a position to provide to their own people standards comparable to those which we might have introduced on only one island? How would we justify our action in other parts of the world where wants and needs were perhaps even greater than they are in some areas of the Commonwealth Caribbean?
Actions which may be taken by a country such as Canada on the international scene will not be viewed in isolation from the general world environment. A moment ago 1 discussed the damage which we might do by expanding our territory into the Caribbean scene. But there is still another factor involved, namely, that of the attitudes of the world community toward small territories which have not yet acceded to independence.
It is now well accepted in international practice that small size or lack of resources should not be an impediment to the obtaining of independence by a people. In the Central Pacific lies the Republic of Nauru with a population of about 6,500. Nauru became independent in 1968, three years after the Maidive Islands which have a population of about 100,000 people. It would surely run counter to a major trend in world affairs if we were to try to alleviate the lot of the inhabitants of small islands in the manner which the motion would seek to do. The day of staking claim to non-contiguous territory, even with the consent of the inhabitants, is well and truly over, for good or for ill.

Canada accepts willingly the concept of assisting its friends in less developed countries throughout the world to achieve acceptable standards of social and economic justice. We will continue to pursue this goal with the tools which we have available or which can further be devised. But absorption will not be one of those tools.
Let me say once again that, while I find the motion unacceptable, it must not be taken that we in any way reject the centuries of friendship which we have enjoyed and which we still very much enjoy with the Commonwealth Caribbean. We admire the peoples of the Commonwealth Caribbean for their industry and talent in creating their own institutions, traditions and cultures. We are jealous of the friendship which we enjoy with the region. It is not to deny any of this that we reject the concept of swallowing up any one of the islands of the Caribbean.
In summary, we should seek to intensify our relations with and assistance to the developing countries in the Caribbean. That is in the spirit of equitable new international economic order. Co-operation and not constitutional absorption are the appropriate ways to work toward a more even-handed world economy.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some degree of pleasure that I rise this afternoon to support my distinguished friend and colleague, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), a noted author and a noted expert on the Caribbean and the so-called West Indies. It is a privilege because he brings to this Chamber with the introduction of his motion, albeit some months ago when snow was on the ground, an awareness of the responsibility that we as Canadians have.
Those of us from the east coast who are maritimers have an awareness of the responsibility that we have to the people lying some 2,000 miles to the south of the east coast of our country. The history of relationships between Canada and those islands is as old or indeed older than Confederation. It is as old as commerce in terms of Canada. In the earliest days our roots, our connections, and our associations with the Caribbean were well established. Those roots and those trade associations continue. I am sure they will continue in the years ahead.
What the hon. member for Hillsborough was attempting to point out is this question of responsibility. The contemporary and recent history of the Caribbean has been one of unsettlement, of striving for determination, of moving from one form of association to another form of association, into independence for some of the islands, and for a continuing status of the islands which he singles out in particular. Those are the islands that are not independent and remain part of the Commonwealth.
Those of us who are maritimers have to be aware of the debt that we owe to the people of the islands. That is the debt which has risen out of our trade with them over the years. We are aware of the friendship they have extended to us, not only as tourists. Tourism in the Caribbean is relatively a new thing in terms of the lengthy history we have in association with the
April 22, 1977

people of those islands. I am referring to the debts that arose out of our common heritage in the Commonwealth, the friendships that developed, and the business associations that were established and continued for well over 150 years. We have firms in the Atlantic provinces which have been doing business with the islands continuously for that period of time. These are associations which in a unique way place us in their debt.
If I understand the plea of the hon. member for Hillsborough through the vehicle of this motion this afternoon, it is to recognize that we do have a debt to these people and we have to do whatever we can to be of assistance to them. One of the forms of assistance could be in the area the motion suggests. 1 find it remarkable, in reviewing the comments made to date with respect to the motion, that the three or four speakers have all said virtually the same thing. 1 could not help but wonder as I read it, who wrote it, because it is obviously a standard response hauled out every once in a while for the convenience of those members who have to sit here on Friday afternoon, 1 imagine largely against their wills.

speechtext: It is the elite of the House you are talking about.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I was not talking about the distinguished Newfoundlanders who feel it a continuous pleasure to sit here. It strikes me that others throw out this package speech whenever necessary, and they use it in order to ensure that ideas such as this one simply do not come to any positive conclusion.
The suggestion that we cannot improve the status of certain people because it might have an effect on neighbouring people seems to me ridiculous, going beyond the request in the motion itself to the hypothetical situation of a union. It seems to me that to reject it because of the reasons put forward by earlier speakers on the government side would be ludicrous. What right do we have, for example, to deny anybody the benefits that could flow from a closer political or economic union with Canada simply because somebody else next door might not like it? I do not think that that argument makes much sense. Indeed it has been suggested by the hon. member for Hillsborough that it is a very narrow and selfish point of view to take. There are many advantages that could accrue to those nonindependent islands from a closer association with Canada. However, that is not what the motion seeks.
I spoke earlier of my perception of the debt we owe these people. I find that one way of discharging that debt, or at least reminding them that we are aware of it, is suggested in the motion, that is, that the matter of a closer political and economic union be studied by a joint committee of the two Houses. If it does nothing else, surely that continues to indicate to the people involved, indeed to the entire Caribbean, that if they ever desire to look to a larger country, a new currency base, a country with modern social programs and institutions already in place, they would know with some certainty that Canadians are interested-not that we would reject them because we can find reasons here and there to say to ourselves that all this would be unfair, that it would be a
West Indies
disadvantage, that it is a very complex thing and we must be careful that we are not hurting others by any precipitous action in this area. That is a hodgepodge of nonsense.
The hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) addressed himself to this matter. I will quote him. I could quote also the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Leblanc) who said much the same thing.
1 quote from Hansard of November 19, 1976, when the matter was introduced and first dealt with in this context. At page 1217 of Hansard we read the following, spoken by the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine:
Even though on the face of it such investments in tourist facilities may seem attractive, the over-all impact must be studied within the context of the total area, like everything else that involves the Commonwealth Caribbean. Increased investments and tourist trade in a given area would most likely deprive other countries of the Commonwealth Caribbean of their revenues from those sources. This would lead to increased unemployment levels and lower living standards in those other countries. Such is certainly not the aim pursued by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie).
He went on to suggest:
This could dry up capital for other Caribbean countries, restraining their traditional share of the Canadian market.
The hon. member went on to suggest a whole lot of dastardly things that could happen because a joint committee of the Parliament of Canada sat down to address itself to these questions in an orderly fashion. I think that is nonsense, and such things would not happen at all.
As much as I may love the Turks and Caicos Islands, whenever 1 get $500 or $600, 1 go to Barbados, and 1 will continue to do that. I have been doing that for 25 or 30 years. That would not divert my money and, even if it did, it would not break them. These arguments are not really to be taken too seriously. 1 do not understand the intransigence of the government with respect to this question.
Again, as pointed out clearly, the intention of the motion is not to enter into a political and economic union but rather to review the matter, to find out whether there is any basis to the allegations brought out by members on the government side. Quite the contrary, I think it is a selfish attitude, as has been said before, to fail to help those who might express a desire for our help simply because that might help somebody else. 1 do not see much logic in that.
For those who are even remotely serious about this question there are a number of useful documents available, and at the risk of a little free publicity here I will draw the attention of hon. members to a book drawing together a series of papers on Canada and the Third World edited by Peyton V. Lyon and Tareg Y. Ismael, published by Macmillan of Canada, in which the distinguished member for Hillsborough deals with the West Indies in great depth, setting them in the context of Canada and the Third World. It is a rather lengthy academic treatment of the subject, but is filled with a lot of useful information. I am sure that if hon. members were to spend an hour or two with it, it might turn around some of their present attitudes with regard to the motion to a position of support for it. I commend to them the section on Canada and the Third

April 22, 1977
West Indies
World entitled "Canada and the Caribbean" written by the distinguished author Macquarrie, scholar and friend, and hon. member for Hillsborough.
Coming back directly to the subject of the motion in front of us it seems to me that there are real barriers in terms of letting this matter go to a further level. For example, we have a few members in this Chamber on the government side who are adamant in not letting the motion go to a committee of the House in its present form. Perhaps some member on the government side, when participating later in the debate, might consider reference of the subject matter of the motion of the hon. member for Hillsborough to a joint committee of the two Houses, or to a committee of this House. But whatever, 1 appeal to hon. members opposite and to the government, at the very least to let us demonstrate and continue to demonstrate to the people of the Caribbean the sincerity of our position with respect to the relationship between our two countries.
Let us at least be given an opportunity to show them that we are serious in these intentions to devote some of our time to looking at their problem in the mid-1970's, to look with some competence at the future which lies ahead for them, to look at their social needs, to look at their needs for upgraded educational standards, to look at their needs for other forms of assistance and help that we can give to them, and not just look at the programs we have going through institutions such as CIDA, CUSO and other groups, and at the private work being done in many of these countries by churches, by educational groups and so on.
Let us consider the benefits we can extend to that part of the world. I urge hon. members not to be caught up with the usual selfish line we get from the government side with respect to this matter. Let us think for a moment or two to see if we can find some way to extend and broaden that great friendship we owe those people, to find a way to demonstrate to them very clearly that should they ever express a desire to find close political and economic ties with this country, at least in this country there would be an open door and a very warm welcome for them.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have wanted to speak on this issue ever since 1 first read about it in the newspapers. That was long before 1 got into politics. 1 quite sincerely find this a startling and alarming proposal. The hon. member's motion raises a subject which has been touched upon in the past in one way or another, and no doubt it is very appealing for busy, frozen Canadians to have delightful thoughts of a warm, tropical island.
The suggestion that a special joint committee be appointed to consider the advisability of taking the initiative to promote closer relations with former British possessions in the West Indies such as the Turks and Caicos Islands goes on to suggest that if the residents of any of these islands so desire, their economic and political union with Canada could be negotiated at an early date. So we have not just a benign proposal here for a committee, but one which suggests leading to some serious
[Mr. Forrestall.)
commitment. The concept embodied in this motion was discussed here in November of last year and in May of 1975, and I personally would have thought that that would have taken care of it very nicely.
Many pros and cons respecting this proposal have already been put forward in this House. I would like, however, to bring out today some points of importance and explain why I believe they represent very serious concerns, certainly to me and, I believe, to others. 1 believe also that the government is serious in resisting these proposals and that it is not just being political.
The suggestion before us is an interesting one which at a first and superficial glance would appear to continue our history of relations with the countries of the Commonwealth Caribbean. I believe, however, that the constitutional step envisaged in the hon. member's motion would not be the culmination but rather a serious distortion and derogation from the established and generally happy modus vivendi between Canada and its fellow Commonwealth members in the Caribbean. That would be a shame.
1 would like to begin by touching briefly on the close relations we have enjoyed for many years with the countries of the Caribbean in various fields; for example, trade and commerce, investment, immigration, transport, tourism and education. In the trade field beneficial relations with our friends in the Commonwealth Caribbean have existed fruitfully for many years, since the days when cod, flour, rum and sugar were the main foundation of a flourishing reciprocal trade.
With the arrival of independence for some of the Caribbean territories and associate statehood for others, we have strengthened those economic ties. As the problems of development have become strongly evident and urgent, we have played an increasingly vigorous part in the fight to overcome a basic problem of insufficient resources for the people in the Caribbean. Many people from the Commonwealth Caribbean have visited Canada, and some have fought in our armed forces, including the Prime Minister of Jamaica, the Hon. Robert Manley, who paid us a very interesting official visit last year.
The exchange of visits between Canadian and Caribbean leaders is a regular feature of our relationship, and the biennial Commonwealth heads of government conferences provide a further chance for informal as well as formal discussions between friends who play important roles in the developed and developing world. At the wider personal level, in the fields of tourism, education, and immigration, the peoples of Canada and the Commonwealth Caribbean have grown to like and help each other. Canada has gained many attractive, worthy and capable citizens from the Commonwealth Caribbean, particularly in the last 15 years, while a number of fortunate Canadians are part-time residents of the Caribbean islands.
In addition to trade and investment, transportation is a further economic link of importance to both sides.
We are now in the process of replacing two old trade agreements, that of 1925 and the 1966 protocol, by an up to date relationship which takes into account realistically the
April 22, 1977

commitments of both sides. Three rounds of consultations have so far taken place, and the processs should be completed this year. As my colleague mentioned, CARICOM, the Caribbean Community and Common Market, would benefit from industrial co-operation, and we hope this will be a feature of our new treaty relationship. I think Canada would probably benefit from that too. As hon. members know, the Caribbean Common Market includes independent states and the six Windward and Leeward Islands, five of which are not yet fully independent but are likely to be so within the next few years.
This is an example of how we are in the process of developing and evolving our relations in the Commonwealth Caribbean in the light of current needs and concepts. We are doing so on the basis of equality and independence, and that needs to be underlined. A step now based on inequality and dependence would cut right across the path we have followed with mutual trust.
I do not believe that we need to, or should, distort and replace this healthy system of natural growth and economic partnership by the unbalanced, one-sided and disproportionate step of legally absorbing into Canada one or more of the small territories which are many miles distant.
Let us consider the effect of the suggested action on the Turks and Caicos Islands. How would the people react and be affected by a legal link with Canada? Would they not be psychologically and sociologically upset by the lifting of all barriers between them and the distant mainland? 1 do not think we know the answers. Would their economy not be strained and distorted by a rush of capital? That may sound like a rather funny suggestion, but in fact there is much experience with this type of problem, particularly in the Third World. Much of the private investment would probably concentrate on tourism, perhaps to the detriment of longer term development projects.
It is true that Canadian government resources for development would be available from DREE and other institutions in an effort to bring the islands up to the level of their Canadian confederation counterparts. Such an effort, however, might create tensions as less developed regions on the Canadian mainland compete for resources with the new Caribbean region. Surely it is within our capability and integral to our heritage as a nation, founded on principles of evolution to independence, to encourage a self-sustaining current of development in these islands and to consider-much less implement-the type of paternalistic structure anticipated by the form of relationship in question. I think that would be inevitable.
The economy of the Turks and Caicos is simple. It encompasses tourism and foreign residents, including Canadians. It is understandable, therefore, that the Turks and Caicos Islands and their people should have a friendly interest in our country. However, if we legally swallowed them, even though at their own wish, we would naturally have to raise their standard of services to Canadian levels. The resulting dissatisfaction in
West Indies
other Caribbean territories with equal or lower per capita incomes would then be inevitable and could sour relations in the area on a wide front. Presumably this would lead to some kind of chain reaction.
Neocolonialism is not a nice word, but the charge of neocolonialism could then be levelled at Canada, of all countries, in various international forums. We are proud of our record in those organizations, and outside them, of strong support for colonial peoples in their advance to self-determination and independence during the last 30 years. It would indeed be a pity if our commendable record in this field were spoiled by misunderstandings created almost inevitably by our constitutional absorption of small territories. This unusual, perhaps anachronistic-we might say "bucking the trend"- step might damage our relationships with other underdeveloped countries which, like the Caribbean, have dealt with us on the basis of mutual consultation and have respected us for our anti-colonial and anti-apartheid policies and for our practice of not making unfair use of our economic strength in our relations with developing countries. Historically it has been Canada's firm belief that the prospect of becoming an imperial power would be detrimental to our traditions and best interests. It is thoroughly un-Canadian.
The hon. member recognizes that this is a complex subject, as is evident by the terms of his proposal. He suggests that Canada should be ready to negotiate economic and political union if so requested by the people of the Caribbean countries concerned. But let us for a moment ponder the possible types of constitutional association the committee would be expected to consider and recommend. Surely we must reject on principle any arrangement which confers an inferior status on the associating territory. Even if this were acceptable and had the support of the local population, the people of the Turks and Caicos, we would be transgressing the fundamental principle of avoiding imperial involvement. We are probably the last country in the world which would want to become involved in that kind of activity. We would not want to do it in an age in which even the smallest of states is regarded as having the right to full independence.
If we, therefore, rule out any form of dependent status, we have the option open to us of conferring full and equal participation in the structure of confederation which, ultimately, would mean full provincial status for the islands. Certainly absorption into an existing province would be impossible, and the arrangements we have made for the Yukon and Northwest Territories, developed as they were in response to the special needs of the north, would not provide a viable precedent in the very different circumstances of the adhesion of new overseas territories to Canada. This applies especially to territories in the tropics. Therefore are we seriously to entertain the prospect of burdening the Turks and Caicos with the full panoply of provincial governments, participation in first ministers' conferences, and consideration of attempts to amend the Canadian constitution? Surely not.
I am well aware that the hon. member is genuinely concerned to ensure that Canada should fill honourably its long-

April 22, 1977
West Indies
standing commitment to good relations with the Commonwealth Caribbean and that we should provide, to the greatest degree possible assistance to the countries of this area at this crucial stage in their evolution. I would submit, however, that this can better be accomplished by means other than a form of constitutional association.
I suppose that is particularly true at the present time, when we are concerned about relations with one of our provinces, Quebec. It is very much to be hoped that the Canadian relationship with the Commonwealth Caribbean will continue to be accorded a high priority among our international commitments. It would, however, manifestly not be in the best interests of the Commonwealth Caribbean if a committee such as the hon. member suggests were established, since such action would be bound to excite interest and speculation in the Commonwealth Caribbean and might tend to detract from the urgent need to deal with Quebec's existing problems. The non-acceptance of this motion would not, I emphasize, in any way indicate a lack of interest by this House in the Commonwealth Caribbean and, most particularly, in the small countries which would have such difficulty in establishing themselves as viable individual entities.
I suggest we must ensure the continuation of the healthy and balanced relationship between Canada and the Commonwealth Caribbean. This must certainly mean the maintenance of an important trading relationship and the continuation of Canada's development assistance program, although the manner of channelling this aid will depend on the particular requirements of individual countries and the evolution of institutions enabling greater regional co-operation. There is nothing new about such ideas. These ideas have been evident in our dealings with countries all around the world, particularly of the Third World. Actually our experience with Third World countries should help us greatly in our dealings with the Commonwealth Caribbean. Of course I refer not only to CARICOM, but to institutions such as the Caribbean Development Bank and the University of the West Indies. Canada has long participated with these organizations to further the economic development and higher education of Caribbean members of the Commonwealth.
Canada will certainly maintain a friendly but not intrusive-and intrusive is the important, operative word-interest in the political as well as economic development within the Commonwealth Caribbean. For the sorts of reasons I have outlined, however, the serious consideration of a constitutional link by a parliamentary committee would not be in the best interests of either the countries in the region or of Canada, and might end up by damaging the good rapport which now exists. Mr. Speaker, for these important reasons I urge the House not to accept the motion.

esting to discuss in the House especially during private members' hour. I think that perhaps the strains of the winter which has just ended have generated some kind of infatuation for the warm countries which permeated his thought when he introduced this motion in the House.
The establishment of economic, political or other ties with those Caribbean islands amuse me, because all the great powers of the world have voluntarily or involuntarily relinquished their possessions. I do not see why Canada, almost as big as a continent, with regional problems and economic disparities throughout its territory, could flirt with the southern islands which would become for us a kind of Hawaii or Florida.
We have no experience of that type of tourist industry, except that Air Canada keeps advertising its "Flights to the 14 suns". They might have to rename it the flights to the 16 suns now, but to my mind this is totally inadequate. In my opinion, instead of being satisfied with leisure trading or trying through other means to send Canadians to spend their winter in those West Indies islands, we should address ourselves to problems of far greater scope in Canada and I have precisely in mind a land issue. Why not improve the land we have, the national capital region-

-where everyone lives in what is called the national capital area? But no one has a thorough knowledge of the history of the national capital area. Nobody knows what troubles people living on the Quebec or Ontario side of the capital area have gone through. We should attempt to find a solution so that within that economic region, which is the same on either side of the Ottawa River, a region agreed upon and set up under an act of Parliament in 1958, and which is called the national capital area, better standards of living might be established. There are large discrepancies, Mr. Speaker, due to the fact that the Canadian Parliament is not located in a region of its own, that it is situated in a province called Ontario. Parliament would be much better off if located in a region of its own, under its full jurisdiction, where it could pass legislation, provide education and become a kind of laboratory. They are dividing the capital of Canada among themselves. And I would be happy if the hon. member for Hillsborough, whose deep knowledge of history is well known, could introduce in the House, especially during private members' hour, either in the form of a motion or simply of a private bill, a measure dealing with the famous question of the national capital region, making it once and for all a kind of federal district so that the capital of Canada can be truly the capital of Canada.

The army is excellent, but its equipment should be renewed, improved, modernized before we go look for islands throughout the world so that Canadians can go there in winter to lay in the sun. 1 encourage them to go to Florida, it is closer, only a three-hour flight, tourism is already organized in Florida and we would spend less money. You can phone there easily. It would be a
West Indies
